- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.33) over recent days, model tends to underreact — adjust forecast upward by 1–3% to compensate for bearish sentiment lag.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >70), model often overcorrects downward — reduce forecast slope by 0.5–1.5% for next 3–5 days to avoid overshoot.
- If official event net supply is negative and bullish sentiment is weak, model underestimates upside — add 2–4% bias to forecast mean for next 5–7 days.
- When sentiment swings from negative to positive (e.g., 0.00 → 0.67), model delays reaction — forecast should rise 1–2% faster than historical trend.
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 65–75 range) after 2–3 spikes, model overestimates mean — cap forecast at 1–2% below recent peak.
- If official events show high bearish balance (≥30) and model forecast is flat, force a 1–3% downward bias to reflect policy-driven supply pressure.
- When sentiment history shows 0.00 for 3+ days, model tends to ignore upcoming events — add 0.5–1.5% upward bias to reflect event-driven volatility.
